card: Paper card. Question: How does the presence of local chemical order (LCO) influence the formation, evolution, and recombination of irradiation-induced point defects and defect clusters in equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloys compared to a random solid solution?. System: Equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA) in two states: water-quenched (approximated as a random solid solution, RSS) and aged at 1,000 °C for 120 h (LCO CrCoNi); pure Ni used as a benchmark.. Processing: Raw ingot homogenized at 1,200 °C for 48 h; split into two treatments: (1) water quenched to room temperature to form RSS; (2) aged at 1,000 °C for 120 h followed by slow furnace cooling to induce LCO. Ion irradiation performed in situ at 300 K using 50 keV He+ ions. Atomistic simulations prepared RSS by random distribution and LCO via MD/MC at 1,300 K with variance-constrained semigrand canonical ensemble.. Test conditions: In situ TEM irradiation at 300 K with 50 keV He+ ions up to 1.0 dpa; MD simulations of primary damage with PKA energies of 5, 10, 20, and 40 keV; diffusion simulations at various temperatures (including 1,200 K) to measure vacancy and interstitial mobility.. Findings: The areal fraction of LCO regions is approximately 3% in water-quenched RSS CrCoNi versus ~30% in the 1,000 °C-aged LCO CrCoNi.; At a low irradiation dose of 0.16 dpa, the LCO sample is nearly defect-free while the RSS sample already contains visible defect clusters.; The number density of defect clusters in the LCO sample is significantly smaller than in the RSS sample across the entire dose range of 0.16 to 1.0 dpa.; The average activation energy for interstitial diffusion increases from 0.22 eV in RSS to 0.34 eV in LCO, while for vacancies it increases from 0.69 eV to 0.76 eV.; The difference in activation energy between interstitial and vacancy diffusion narrows from 0.47 eV in RSS to 0.42 eV in LCO, reducing the mobility ratio.; The correlation factor for interstitial diffusion decreases by 29% (from 0.232 to 0.165) in LCO compared to RSS, indicating stronger localization of interstitial motion.; Large-sized defect clusters (Ncluster > 30) are suppressed in LCO CrCoNi, with the number of point defects in large clusters being ~35% lower than in RSS.; The recombination rate of Frenkel pairs at the end of the thermal spike is nearly identical for RSS and LCO (~99.6%), but the LCO sample retains fewer surviving FPs due to enhanced recombination during the cooling phase.. Mechanism: The authors argue that LCO enhances irradiation resistance through a two-pronged kinetic effect: (1) it increases migration energy barriers, slowing down the diffusion of both vacancies and interstitials (localizing their motion); and (2) it narrows the mobility ratio between interstitials and vacancies (by affecting interstitials more strongly), which increases the probability of their recombination and annihilation during the cooling phase of the collision cascade, thereby reducing the number of surviving defects and large clusters.. Limitations: The study notes that small-sized defect clusters (Ncluster < 8) are not detectable by in-situ TEM due to resolution limits and are susceptible to dissolution, so the comparison between experiment and simulation focuses on large-sized clusters. The extent of LCO investigated is limited to chemical short-range order (CSRO) developed via the specific aging treatment.. Future work: The authors propose that tailoring composition and heat treatment to extend LCO beyond CSRO into medium-range or long-range order, or adding interstitial alloying elements (such as C, N) with chemical affinity for specific constituents, could further boost irradiation tolerance.. Quote: "increased local chemical order (e.g., via thermal aging) significantly enhances their resistance to irradiation damage by narrowing the mobility ratio of irradiation-induced interstitials and vacancies that can facilitate their recombination."
W4362523442.title: Effect of local chemical order on the irradiation-induced defect evolution in CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy

card: Paper card. Question: How do the strength, ductility, and fracture toughness of an equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy compare to high-entropy alloys and conventional materials, particularly at cryogenic temperatures, and what mechanisms drive these properties?. System: Equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA). Processing: Arc-melted high-purity elements (>99.9%) under argon, drop-cast into copper moulds, homogenized at 1,200 °C for 24 h, cold-forged and cross-rolled to ~10 mm thickness (60% reduction), then annealed at 800 °C for 1 h in air to achieve a recrystallized microstructure with 5–50 μm grains.. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests at 293 K, 198 K, and 77 K with a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹; Compact-tension (C(T)) fracture toughness tests at 293 K, 198 K, and 77 K with fatigue pre-cracking and side-grooving per ASTM E1820.. Findings: At 77 K, yield strength reached 657 MPa and ultimate tensile strength reached 1,311 MPa, representing a ~50% increase from room temperature.; Tensile ductility (failure strain) increased to ~0.9 (90%) at 77 K, a ~25% increase from room temperature.; Fracture toughness (KJIc) at crack initiation increased from 208 MPa m1/2 at 293 K to 273 MPa m1/2 at 77 K.; Crack-growth toughness at 77 K reached critical stress-intensity values of ~430 MPa m1/2 (J ~900 kJ m⁻²).; The alloy exhibited a high strain-hardening exponent (n) of 0.4 at cryogenic temperatures.; The CrCoNi alloy showed ~15% higher tensile strength, ~30% higher ductility, and ~50% higher work of fracture than the five-component CrMnFeCoNi alloy at room temperature.; At 77 K, the CrCoNi alloy displayed ~25% higher KJIc, ~27% higher ductility, and ~31% higher work of fracture compared to the CrMnFeCoNi alloy.. Mechanism: The exceptional damage tolerance results from continuous steady strain hardening that suppresses plastic instability, driven by pronounced dislocation activity and deformation-induced nano-twinning. Nano-twinning acts as a dominant deformation mode that provides a steady source of strain hardening, delaying necking and accommodating strain, with its intensity increasing as temperature decreases from room temperature to 77 K.. Limitations: The yield strength at 77 K was slightly lower than the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, attributed to the non-uniform grain size of the current material; the volume fraction of void-initiating inclusions was not accurately quantified relative to the five-component alloy.. Future work: Further studies are needed to accurately determine the relative volume fractions of void-initiating inclusions in the MEA and HEA and to identify their chemistry and crystal structure by TEM after extraction from the voids.. Quote: "strength, ductility and toughness of the CrCoNi alloy improve to strength levels above 1.3 GPa, failure strains up to 90% and KJIc values of 275 MPa m1/2."

card: Paper card. Question: What distinguishes multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) from traditional solid solutions, and how does local chemical order (LCO) influence dislocation behavior and mechanical strength?. System: FCC NiCoCr medium-entropy alloy (equiatomic composition). Processing: Hybrid molecular dynamics (MD) and Monte Carlo (MC) simulations with annealing temperatures (Ta) ranging from 650 K to 1650 K; empirical embedded-atom method (EAM) potential developed without spin polarization; simulation box ~52 nm × 6 nm × 52 nm with 1,584,000 atomic sites; 270,000–500,000 MC cycles for convergence.. Test conditions: Energy pathway calculations at 0 K; dislocation motion simulations at 300 K under constant shear stress of 300 MPa; strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1 for CRSS estimation; activation barrier calculations via minimum energy path (MEP).. Findings: Configurational entropy (Sc) rarely reaches the ideal value (Sc,ideal); at 1650 K, Sc is ~95% of Sc,ideal, but drops significantly as LCO develops at lower Ta.; Complex stacking fault energy (CSFE) varies from -24.0 mJ/m² (random solid solution) to ~57 mJ/m² (strong LCO at 650 K).; Local antiphase boundary energies (APBEs) increase from ~50 mJ/m² to ~112 mJ/m² as Ta decreases from 1650 K to 650 K.; Twin boundary energy (γB) in LCO samples increases linearly with the number of transformed layers (λ), unlike elemental FCC metals where it converges.; Dislocations move via intermittent nanoscale segment detrapping (NSD) rather than smooth propagation, with effective barriers of ~0.15 eV even at 400 MPa shear stress.; Shear stress required to drive dislocation motion increases by a factor of three when the alloy is annealed at 650 K compared to the random state.; Critical resolved shear strength (CRSS) for the random NiCoCr state is ~70 MPa at 300 K and 10^-3 s^-1, consistent with experimental values of ~69 ± 3 MPa.. Mechanism: LCO creates a rugged energy landscape with spatially heterogeneous complex stacking fault energies (CSFE) and antiphase boundary energies (APBE). This heterogeneity acts as nanoscale obstacles that trap dislocation segments, forcing them to move via a nanoscale segment detrapping (NSD) mechanism. The energy required to break LCOs during slip and twinning increases activation barriers and lattice friction, leading to strengthening.. Limitations: The study uses a non-magnetic EAM potential which does not explicitly consider spin polarization; magnetic effects could alter energy differences by ~15 meV/atom. The simulations assume a single-phase solution without second-phase precipitation. Kinetic limitations in experiments may prevent the formation of predicted LCO states at low temperatures within typical homogenization times.. Future work: The authors propose using rapid cooling to obtain a random solid solution for ductility, followed by aging at elevated temperatures to induce LCO for strength. They suggest that the variability in LCO offers a new knob for property tuning in single-phase alloys.. Quote: "The LCO heightens the ruggedness of the energy landscape and raises activation barriers governing dislocation activities."

Paper card. Question: How does local chemical order (LCO) affect local dislocation segment activation barriers in multi-principal element alloys?. System: Multi-principal element alloys (specifically samples with equilibrium LCOs at Ta = 650, 950, and 1350 K). Processing: Hybrid MD and MC simulations on 20 nm × 20 nm × 10 nm samples (30 samples per condition) at Ta = 650, 950, and 1350 K; quenched to 0 K; cylinder configurations (20 nm diameter, 10 nm length) cut with a partial dislocation of screw character introduced; quasi-static athermal shearing employed; MEPs calculated using the simplified and improved string method with FIRE algorithm (reparameterization every 10 increments, convergence <10–3 Å or 3000 iterations). Test conditions: Temperatures of 650 K, 950 K, and 1350 K for equilibrium LCO; 0 K for energy minimization; athermal stress limit via quasi-static shearing. Findings: 30 different samples were obtained for each processing condition to ensure meaningful statistics; Sample dimensions were 20 nm × 20 nm × 10 nm along x[11¯0], y[1¯1¯1¯], and z[112¯]; Cylinder configurations had a diameter of 20 nm and axial direction along [112¯]; Dislocation line length was 10 nm as detrapping processes are on the nanoscale; Outer layers of atoms with thickness >2x potential cutoff radius were fixed during energy minimization; Inner cylindrical region with 10 nm diameter was used to calculate average local shear stress; Convergence criterion for MEP calculation was displacement <10–3 Å or 3000 iterations. Mechanism: The authors employed hybrid MD and MC simulations to obtain equilibrium LCOs and then used the string method to calculate minimum energy pathways (MEPs) for dislocation segments, aiming to examine LCO effects on local dislocation segment activation barriers.. Quote: "In order to examine the LCO effects on local dislocation segment activation barriers, hybrid MD and MC simulations were performed"

card: Paper card. Question: How does chemical short-range order (SRO) affect the mobility mechanisms of screw and edge dislocations in the MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) across a wide temperature range?. System: MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA), specifically comparing random solid solution (RSS) and equilibrium SRO states at 800 K. Processing: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using a moment tensor potential (MTP) machine-learning interatomic potential; SRO states equilibrated via hybrid MD/Monte Carlo (MD/MC) approach at 800 K. Test conditions: Temperatures from 300 K to 2000 K; applied shear stresses ranging from 0 to 3.0 GPa for screws and 0 to 1.0 GPa for edges; dislocation line length ~15 nm. Findings: At 300 K, SRO provides an extra strengthening of ~180 MPa for screw dislocations due to the formation of diffuse antiphase boundaries (DAPBs).; The strengthening effect of SRO on screw dislocations attenuates with increasing temperature, becoming negligible at 2000 K where mobility curves for RSS and SRO samples overlap.; A cross-slip locking mechanism involving the formation of jogs is observed for screw dislocations, providing extra strengthening independent of SRO presence.; Unlike screw dislocations, the mobility of edge dislocations is enhanced by the presence of SRO, particularly in the high-stress regime.; The SRO-induced enhancement of edge dislocation mobility extends to a characteristic length scale of approximately 1.2 nm into neighboring planes.; At 300 K, dislocation velocities in the MoNbTaW RHEA are significantly lower than in pure Mo and Nb, but this difference diminishes at 2000 K.; The attenuation of SRO strengthening at high temperatures is attributed to the increasing contribution of the entropy term (ΔS_kp) to the kink-pair formation free energy.. Mechanism: For screw dislocations, SRO creates an energy barrier (DAPB formation energy) that must be overcome during kink-pair nucleation, causing strengthening that is thermally activated and thus diminishes at high temperatures. For edge dislocations, SRO flattens the energy landscape, reducing solute drag effects and enhancing mobility despite the energy cost of disrupting order on the slip plane. Cross-slip locking in screws involves the formation of jogs on different slip planes that pin the dislocation line.. Limitations: The simulations use short dislocation line lengths (~15 nm) compared to realistic experimental conditions, meaning calculated velocities are dependent on this size and cannot be directly compared to macroscopic theoretical models without extrapolation. The study assumes the SRO state remains fixed during dislocation motion and does not account for changes in ordering around the moving core.. Future work: The authors state that predicting how the identified mechanisms combine to determine material strength requires appealing to mesoscale models for longer dislocation lengths and longer timescales, which is beyond the scope of the current work.. Quote: "The mobility of edge dislocations is found to be enhanced by the presence of SRO, whereas the rate of double-kink nucleation in the motion of screw dislocations is reduced."

Paper card. Question: How does chemical short-range order (SRO) and temperature affect the mobility and friction stress of edge versus screw dislocations in a bcc MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) compared to pure bcc metals and binary alloys?. System: MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA), pure Mo, and binary Mo-Nb alloys (Mo95Nb5 to Mo75Nb25). Processing: Machine-learning interatomic potential (MTP) with radius cutoff (Rcut) of 4.7 Å and maximum level (levmax) of 14; MC/MD equilibration at 800 K; dislocation mobility simulations using LAMMPS with shear stress ramped at 20 MPa per 1.5 ps and held for 150 ps at temperatures of 300 K and 2000 K. Test conditions: Temperatures: 300 K and 2000 K; Shear stress ramp rate: 20 MPa per 1.5 ps; Hold time: 150 ps; Critical friction stress defined at 0.2 Å/ps for screw and 1.0 Å/ps for edge dislocations. Findings: The edge-to-screw velocity ratio decreases from 20 at 300 K to 11 at 2000 K in MoNbTaW.; Critical friction stress for edge dislocations decreases by 140 MPa from 300 to 2000 K.; Critical friction stress for screw dislocations decreases by 1.3 GPa (an order of magnitude larger) from 300 to 2000 K.; At ~2000 K, the critical friction stresses for both edge and screw dislocations decay to approximately the same level.; SRO hinders screw dislocation motion but accelerates edge dislocation motion in the RHEA.; A novel cross-slip locking mechanism was observed in the RHEA, attributed to intrinsic energy fluctuations and rugged energy landscapes.; Critical stress for screw dislocations follows an exponential decay with temperature, while edge dislocations follow a linear decrease.; Binary Mo-Nb alloys show lower critical friction stresses compared to the RHEA, with edge friction converging to zero in pure bcc metals.. Mechanism: Screw dislocations move via kink-pair nucleation and migration; SRO increases the free-energy barrier for kink-pair nucleation, causing temperature-dependent strengthening. Edge dislocations are accelerated by SRO through the attenuation of solute interaction magnitudes. The cross-slip locking mechanism arises from intrinsic energy fluctuations along the dislocation line and the rugged energy landscape.. Limitations: The study notes that the cross-slip locking mechanism was observed even with a limited cell size, implying potential size effects, and the phenomenological model is constructed specifically for the double-kink mechanism.. Future work: The authors state that the findings demonstrate mechanisms that can have a significant impact on mechanical properties, implying future work should explore these impacts, though no specific future experiments are explicitly detailed in the provided text.. Quote: "The edge-to-screw mobility ratio is around 20 at 300 K, which decreases to 11 when the temperature is raised to 2000 K."

card: Paper card. Question: How can a high-entropy alloy be designed to simultaneously achieve high yield strength and high crack-initiation fracture toughness, overcoming the typical trade-off between these properties?. System: Al0.5CrCoFeNi high-entropy alloy (composition: Cr ~22.5%, Co ~24.6%, Fe ~23.2%, Ni ~24.5%, Al ~5.21 wt%). Processing: Laser powder-bed fusion (L-PBF) additive manufacturing using an Nd:YAG fiber laser (300 W power, 50 µm layer thickness, 90 µm hatch spacing, 500 mm.s−1 scanning speed) followed by optional heat treatments (e.g., 750 °C for 1 h). Test conditions: Tensile tests at 298 K and 77 K with strain rate 10−3 s−1; Fracture toughness tests (C(T) specimens) at 298 K and 77 K using J-integral-based R-curves. Findings: Yield strength (σy) of as-printed alloy is ~729 ± 31 MPa at 298 K and ~942 ± 11 MPa at 77 K.; Crack-initiation fracture toughness (KJIc) is ~306 MPa√m at 298 K and ~290 MPa√m at 77 K.; The as-printed alloy shows ~47% higher KJIc than wrought CrCoNi at 298 K.; The as-printed alloy shows ~66% higher yield strength than wrought CrCoNi at 298 K.; Heat treatment (HT3: 750 °C, 1 h) increases yield strength to ~1090 MPa at 298 K but reduces KJIc to ~135 MPa√m.; At 77 K, the heat-treated alloy exhibits unstable crack growth with KJIc dropping to ~51 MPa√m.; Dislocation bands spread up to ~300 µm away from the crack tip in the as-printed honeycomb microstructure.; Nano-twinning is activated at 77 K in the as-printed alloy, with twin growth restricted by B2 phase boundaries.. Mechanism: The nano-bridged honeycomb microstructure provides strength via the ordered B2 phase and high dislocation density, while the dislocation nano-bridges connecting the B2 phase on cell boundaries act as highways for dislocation movement away from the crack tip, facilitating crack blunting and shielding to enhance intrinsic toughness.. Limitations: Conventional heat treatments that form uniformly distributed B2 precipitates restrict dislocation movement away from the crack tip, leading to a significant reduction in fracture toughness (e.g., ~5.7 times lower at 77 K compared to the as-printed state).. Future work: Manipulating the thermal gradient (G) and solidification rate (R) during 3D printing to alter the size of the honeycomb cells and tailor the material's strength and fracture toughness for specific applications.. Quote: "The dislocation nano-bridge form in the regions of the cell boundaries where solutes (Al/Ni) concentration was insufficient to the form B2 phase."

card: Paper card. Question: How can fatigue life be enhanced in high-entropy alloys at low strain amplitudes without sacrificing ductility, specifically by addressing the trade-off between fatigue strength and fatigue-crack-initiation resistance in precipitation-strengthened alloys?. System: Al0.5CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy containing an FCC matrix and multicomponent B2 precipitates (NiAl-type). Processing: Vacuum-induction melting to fabricate a large plate, followed by hot rolling with 60% reduction at 1150 °C, and annealing at 1000 °C for 1 h. Test conditions: Monotonic tension at RT with a strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; fully-reversed strain-controlled low-cycle fatigue (LCF) at RT with strain amplitudes from ±0.1% to ±1.75% and a strain rate of 1 × 10−2 s−1; real-time in situ neutron diffraction at strain amplitudes of ±0.5%, ±1%, and ±1.75%. Findings: The alloy exhibits at least four times longer fatigue life than conventional alloys at a plastic strain amplitude of ~0.03%.; The B2 phase bears significantly more stress than the FCC phase after yielding, with lattice strains nearly ten times larger.; Stress-induced martensitic transformation (SIMT) occurs in the B2 phase, evidenced by abnormal peak broadening and peak separation in neutron diffraction.; Deformation twinning is observed in the FCC matrix only at high strain amplitudes (≥1.75%), not at intermediate amplitudes (1%).; The B2 phase is plastically deformable at all tested strain amplitudes, storing dislocations and relieving stress concentration.; Fine B2 precipitates act as efficient crack arresters, forming blunted cracks, whereas coarse band-like B2 precipitates initiate microcracks.; The multicomponent B2 phase has lower antiphase boundary (APB) energies (e.g., compared to 0.697 eV/m² for pure NiAl) enabling plastic deformation.. Mechanism: The enhanced fatigue life is attributed to the ductile-transformable character of the multicomponent B2 precipitates, which undergo reversible martensitic transformation and plastic deformation to accommodate strain incompatibility with the FCC matrix. This mechanism relieves stress concentration at phase boundaries, retards microcrack initiation, and provides alternative deformation pathways, unlike brittle traditional intermetallics.. Limitations: The study notes that if the B2 phase size is too large (e.g., band-like precipitates), it becomes easy to initiate microcracks due to longer incoherent interfaces where stress concentration cannot be effectively accommodated.. Future work: The authors propose that the design strategy of introducing ductile-transformable multicomponent intermetallic precipitates can guide the design of fatigue-resistant alloys by tuning HEA compositions and thermomechanical processing.. Quote: "the current HEA shows at least four times longer life than conventional alloys"
W3169352931.title: Enhancing fatigue life by ductile-transformable multicomponent B2 precipitates in a high-entropy alloy

card: Paper card. Question: How do the dual roles of grain boundaries as dislocation obstacles and sources weigh against each other to determine toughness and the brittle-to-ductile transition, and can this explain the minimum in toughness at an intermediate grain size?. System: Pure tungsten (model material for polycrystalline tungsten). Processing: Two-dimensional discrete dislocation dynamics modelling; parameters varied: mean free path for dislocation glide (δ), obstacle force (ϕ), and dislocation source spacing (λ); simulations run at 200–800 K with loading rate K˙ = 1 MPa m0.5/s. Test conditions: Temperature range 200–800 K; applied stress intensity raised at constant rate; critical stress intensity KIC = 2 MPa m0.5; obstacle force varied from 0.1 to 1000 GPa; source spacing λ varied from 0 to 1000 nm. Findings: For materials where λ is the mean distance of intrinsic sources and grain boundaries confine the plastic zone, decreasing grain size (decreasing δ) results in decreased toughness.; For materials where λ is the mean distance of grain boundary intersections with the crack front, a simultaneous decrease of δ and λ results in increased toughness.; The positive impact of grain boundaries (as sources) outweighs the negative impact (as obstacles) when λ is dominated by grain boundary intersections.; Toughness passes through a minimum at an intermediate grain size where the relevant measure for λ transitions from intrinsic sources to grain boundary intersections.; The brittle-to-ductile transition temperature passes through a maximum at an intermediate grain size, mirroring the toughness minimum.; In cold-worked metals with elongated grains, increasing the grain aspect ratio increases the anisotropy of fracture toughness.; The derived relationship for grain-size-dependent fracture toughness is K(dδ, dλ) = KIC + kdδ0.5/dλ.. Mechanism: Grain boundaries act as both obstacles (reducing mean free path δ and promoting pile-ups that suppress dislocation nucleation) and sources (intersection points with the crack front reduce source spacing λ, promoting shielding and blunting). The dominant mechanism depends on grain size: in coarse grains, intrinsic sources dominate (λ constant, δ decreases with grain size, toughness drops); in fine grains, grain boundary intersections dominate (λ decreases with grain size, toughness rises). The transition between these regimes creates a minimum in toughness and a maximum in BDT temperature.. Limitations: The study uses a two-dimensional model; the BDT temperature determination combines numerical toughness data with experimental yield stress data without fitting, yielding only semi-quantitative results; the model assumes λ and ϕ are independent of temperature.. Future work: The authors propose refining the working hypothesis on mechanisms controlling the BDT of pre-deformed, textured, polycrystalline body-centred cubic metals based on the harmonized explanation of contradictory experimental results.. Quote: "Our results show that for materials or microstructures for which the mean distance of the intersection points of grain boundaries with the crack front is the relevant measure for λ, a decrease of grain size results in an increase of toughness."

Paper card. Question: To identify the grain-size-dependence of toughness, K=K(d), and the BDT temperature, TBDT=TBDT(d), which was an open question before.. Processing: Two-dimensional discrete dislocation dynamics modelling with parameter studies varying: (i) mean free path for dislocation glide, δ, (ii) obstacle force of the grain boundary, ϕ, and (iii) dislocation source spacing along the crack front, λ.. Test conditions: Case study I: varied δ while holding others constant. Case study II: varied λ while holding others constant. Case study III: simultaneously varied δ and λ.. Findings: A decrease of the mean free path for dislocation glide, δ (a decrease of grain size) results in a decrease of toughness.; A decrease of the dislocation source spacing along the crack front, λ (a decrease of grain size) results in an increase of toughness.; The simultaneous decrease of λ and δ results in an increase of toughness.; Under these test conditions, grain boundaries are always positive, or at least neutral.; Toughness passes through a minimum (and the BDT temperature passes through a maximum) at an intermediate grain size.; The relevant measure for λ changes with decreasing grain size from 'the mean distance of the intrinsic sources along the crack front' to 'the mean distance of intersection points of grain boundaries with the crack front'.. Mechanism: Grain boundaries act as both obstacles for dislocation glide (reducing toughness) and preferred dislocation nucleation sites at the crack front (increasing toughness). At large grain sizes, intrinsic sources dominate and grain size reduction reduces toughness; at small grain sizes, boundary intersections dominate and grain size reduction increases toughness, creating a minimum in toughness at an intermediate critical grain size.. Quote: "The aim of this paper was to identify the grain-size-dependence of toughness, K=K(d), and the BDT temperature, TBDT=TBDT(d), which was an open question before."

Question: How can a single-phase high-entropy intermetallic alloy be designed to overcome the inherent brittleness of traditional intermetallics and achieve both high strength and extensive plasticity at room temperature and high homologous temperatures?. System: (CoNi)50(TiZrHf)50 (at. %) single-phase B2 high-entropy intermetallic alloy. Processing: Arc-melting high-purity raw materials (>99.9 wt.%) under Ti-gettered argon atmosphere, remelted at least five times, drop-cast into a copper mold, homogenized at 1000 °C for 24 h, and water quenched. Test conditions: Uniaxial compression from room temperature to ~0.9Tm (1582 K) at 1 × 10−3 s−1; microcompression on 1 μm diameter pillars at RT, 573 K, and 673 K; in situ STEM at RT and 573 K. Findings: Yield strength of ~1.5 GPa with plastic strain of ~8% at room temperature, which is about eight times that of conventional B2 alloys like NiAl and CoTi.; The alloy exhibits no precipitous thermal softening between homologous temperatures of 0.5 and 0.7, maintaining strength and strain hardening up to ~0.7Tm.; Micropillars with [100], [110], and [111] orientations show similar yield strength and elastic stiffness, indicating isotropic-like mechanical behavior.; Two slip systems, {110}<111> and {010}<100>, were identified with critical resolved shear stresses of 1235 ± 39 MPa and 1176 ± 245 MPa, respectively, differing by only 5%.; At room temperature, deformation induces local amorphization within slip bands, whereas at temperatures above 573 K, deformation results in dense dislocation forests without amorphization.; The velocity ratio of screw-to-edge dislocations was calculated to be ~0.6 at 300 K, significantly higher than the ~0.2 ratio in brittle BCC metals like tungsten.. Mechanism: Severe lattice distortion caused by atomic size and electronic property misfit mitigates atomic bonding differences along various crystal orientations, enabling dislocation multiplicity and isotropic behavior. Dislocation gliding disturbs the local chemical order, causing structural instability that leads to amorphization at low temperatures and the formation of local crystal-like order (dynamic hardening) at high temperatures, which impedes subsequent dislocation gliding and stabilizes plastic flow.. Limitations: The text notes that fracture at low temperatures may occur within amorphized regions and that the plastic strain at room temperature can vary (up to 27%) depending on machine stiffness, though this variability disappears at higher temperatures.. Future work: The authors suggest that manipulating the lattice distortion by adjusting the ratio of Co to Ni is a topic that warrants further research but is out of the scope of the current work.. Quote: "Unlike conventional intermetallics, this high-entropy alloy features a highly distorted crystalline lattice with complex chemical order, leading to multiple slip systems and high flow stress."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the physical origins of the exceptional high-temperature strength and strength retention in refractory body-centered-cubic (BCC) high-entropy alloys (HEAs)?. System: NbTaTiV (nominal Nb25Ta25Ti25V25 at.%) and CrMoNbV (nominal CrMoNbV at.%); search space includes the 10-component Al-Cr-Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-V-W-Zr family.. Processing: Arc-melting of 99.9 wt.% purity elements under argon atmosphere followed by drop-casting into cylindrical rods; NbTaTiV homogenized at 1473 K for 3 days then water-cooled; CrMoNbV tested in the as-cast state.. Test conditions: Uniaxial compression at strain rates of 1 × 10−3 s−1 (NbTaTiV) and 2 × 10−4 s−1 (CrMoNbV); temperatures up to 1173 K; in situ neutron diffraction and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) performed during deformation.. Findings: Neutron diffraction peak broadening analysis yielded q values of -0.6 to -0.4 for NbTaTiV and -2 for CrMoNbV, consistent with edge dislocations and distinct from screw dislocations (+1.9 to +2.1).; Bright-field STEM stereographic analysis of NbTaTiV deformed at 293 K showed 75% (58 of 77) of dislocations were of edge character.; Bright-field STEM stereographic analysis of CrMoNbV deformed at 293 K showed 56% (23 of 41) of dislocations were of edge character.; At 1173 K, edge dislocations remained dominant with 82% (27 of 33) in NbTaTiV and 64% (81 of 127) in CrMoNbV.; The CrMoNbV alloy exhibited the highest reported strength at a homologous temperature of 1173 K.; A computationally guided search over 10^7 BCC HEA compositions identified over 10^6 possible ultra-strong high-temperature alloy compositions.; Theoretical predictions for NbTaTiV strength were lower than experimental values by ~300-500 MPa, attributed to 1.6 at.% O+N interstitial impurities.. Mechanism: In complex HEAs, fluctuations in local solute arrangements create large local variations in potential energy, forcing edge dislocations to adopt a low-energy wavy structure; plastic flow requires thermal activation to overcome large energy barriers created by adjacent high-energy environments, enabling high strength retention at elevated temperatures.. Limitations: The theory does not capture the strength plateau observed at 973–1273 K in many BCC HEAs; neutron pattern quality for CrMoNbV was lower than for NbTaTiV, especially at low plastic strains; the theory assumes a homogeneous average alloy which may not fully capture local complexities.. Future work: Propose fabrication and testing of specific alloys (Mo5W2.5CrZrHf, Mo2.5W2.5CrZrHf, Mo6WCrZrHf, Mo2.5TaWV2.5CrZrHf) with predicted strengths of ~2.5-3 GPa at 1300 K; combine design strategy with detailed thermodynamics and high ductility criteria to discover multi-objective alloys.. Quote: "Here we show, using integrated in-situ neutron-diffraction (ND), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), and recent theory, that the high strength and strength retention of a NbTaTiV alloy and a high-strength/low-density CrMoNbV alloy are attributable to edge dislocations."

card: Paper card. Question: How does temperature influence the transition between smooth (mild) and intermittent (wild) plastic flow in body-centered cubic (bcc) Niobium, and what is the underlying dislocation mechanism governing this bimodal behavior?. System: Single-crystal Niobium (Nb), commercially pure, oriented along the ⟨123⟩ direction. Processing: Focused ion beam (FIB) milling to fabricate cylindrical microcrystals (height 6 μm, diameter 2 μm); uniaxial microcompression testing at a displacement rate of 0.6 nm s⁻¹ (strain rate 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹) across temperatures of 173–368 K; 3D discrete dislocation dynamics (DDD) simulations using the MODELib package at strain rates of 718 s⁻¹ and 7180 s⁻¹. Test conditions: Temperatures: 173 K, 263 K, 298 K, 323 K, 368 K; Strain rates: 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ (experiment), 718 s⁻¹ and 7180 s⁻¹ (simulation); Loading axis: ⟨123⟩; Slip system: {211}⟨111⟩. Findings: Plasticity is bimodal, consisting of thermally activated smooth flow ('mild') and athermal intermittent bursts ('wild') that coexist across the temperature regime.; The effective barrier energy for athermal dislocation avalanches is 0.04 eV, which is an order of magnitude smaller than the 0.3 eV barrier energy for smooth plastic flow at 298 K.; The distribution of avalanche sizes shifts from a scale-free power law at 298–368 K to an exponential (Weibull) distribution at 173 K, with a characteristic length scale of ~0.3 nm.; The fraction of athermal slip activity (η) increases markedly at the critical temperature Tc (approx. 290–320 K), where screw and edge dislocation mobilities equalize.; DDD simulations confirm that screw dislocations are the dominant segment type (>90%) in avalanches, despite the observed athermal behavior.; Screw dislocations involved in avalanches are subjected to local stresses significantly exceeding the Peierls stress (τ > τP), neutralizing their thermal sensitivity.; The proportion of athermal strain contribution decreases with decreasing temperature due to a reduction in the effective screening length for elastic coupling.. Mechanism: The authors argue that athermal screw dislocation slip is driven by the emergence of local stresses in screw dislocation pileups that exceed the Peierls stress (τP). When τ > τP, screw dislocations exhibit viscous motion similar to edge dislocations, effectively bypassing the classical thermally activated kink-pair nucleation mechanism. As temperature decreases, the Peierls potential increases, reducing the 'screening distance' (2d0) for elastic coupling between dislocations, which suppresses the length scale of avalanches and transitions the statistics from scale-free to exponential.. Limitations: The experimental sensor resolution limits the ability to detect rearrangements smaller than the current noise threshold (~0.165 nm), preventing observation of potential single-armed spiral source activity at very low temperatures. Additionally, the DDD simulations were performed at strain rates (718 s⁻¹) much higher than experimental rates (10⁻⁴ s⁻¹), though the authors note the strain-rate sensitivity exponents match.. Future work: The authors suggest that verifying the activity of single-armed spiral sources at very low temperatures would require nanomechanical testing with displacement resolution higher than current state-of-the-art capabilities. They also propose that the ratio of athermal to total plastic strain (η) could serve as a direct experimental method to determine the critical temperature Tc.. Quote: "Plasticity is shown to be bimodal across the studied temperature regime, with conventional thermally-activated smooth plastic flow ('mild') coexisting with sporadic bursts ('wild') controlled by athermal screw dislocation activity."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the nature of the polyamorphic transition (PT) in high-entropy metallic glasses (HEMGs) compared to conventional metallic glasses, and how does high configurational entropy influence the transition mechanism and resulting glass states?. System: Ti20Zr20Hf20Cu20Ni20 (atomic ratio) high-entropy metallic glass (HEMG). Processing: Vacuum arc melting of high-purity elements followed by re-melting at least four times; melt-spinning to produce 30 μm thick ribbons; subsequent reheating to specific temperatures (713, 726, 740, 753, and 771 K) and quenching to room temperature to generate intermediate glass states (Gm1-4) and a final state (Gn).. Test conditions: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) at 0.17 K s−1; in-situ heating synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD) at 0.17 K s−1; temperature-modulated DSC (TMDSC) at 2 K min−1 with 1 K amplitude; high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM); small-angle neutron scattering (SANS); atom probe tomography (APT); EXAFS at Cu, Ni, and Zr K-edges; nanoindentation at 0.05 s−1 strain rate.. Findings: The PT in Ti20Zr20Hf20Cu20Ni20 HEMG is a continuous polyamorphic transition (CPT) occurring between 697 K and 771 K, lacking first-order characteristics like abrupt volume or energy reduction.; Multiple distinct glass states (Gm1-4 and Gn) with identical composition but different thermodynamic properties and glass transition temperatures (Tg) ranging from 637 K to 694 K were generated.; The linear expansion coefficient below 575 K is (2.45 ± 0.03) × 10−5 K−1, while above 697 K, a gradual volume decrease of approximately 0.25% occurs without abrupt changes.; Atomic structural ordering increases during CPT, evidenced by a decrease in the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the first diffraction peak from 0.388 Å−1 to 0.365 Å−1.; Chemical heterogeneity increases during CPT, with Ni distribution deviating from a binomial distribution in the final state (Gn), showing significant density fluctuations.; The Warren-Cowley parameter (αij) for Ni-Zr pairs decreases from −0.029 to −0.048, indicating enhanced chemical short-range order.; Hardness and modulus increase by approximately 25% as a function of the increasing Tg resulting from the CPT process.; The characteristic time of the CPT is relatively large, with the process continuing for approximately 6.4 × 104 s even above the transition onset temperature.. Mechanism: The continuous transformation is driven by the high configurational entropy which initially homogenizes the structure and limits the distance and frequency of atomic diffusion. Upon heating, the system undergoes continuous atomic shuffling within the nearest neighbor shell to form locally favored structures with enhanced chemical ordering (specifically Ni-Zr bonds), while atomic rearrangements at larger length scales are suppressed. This results in a continuous reduction of excess configurational entropy and a progressive densification without the nucleation and growth of a distinct second glass phase typical of first-order transitions.. Limitations: The text notes that the CPT is kinetically frustrated and that the atomic structure has a weak dependence on temperature due to limited translational degrees of freedom in the supercooled liquid region. It also mentions that atomic size misfit and enthalpy also influence CPT, though the focus is on configurational entropy.. Future work: The authors propose that the CPT phenomenon provides a model system for investigating the fundamental principles of glass states, such as glass transition and glass-forming ability, and for exploring structure-property relationships. They suggest the discovery offers opportunities to tune glassy structures and properties of HEMGs without altering chemical composition.. Quote: "This CPT behavior is featured by the continuous structural evolution at the atomic level and an increasing chemical concentration gradient with temperature, but no abrupt reduction in volume and energy."

card: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy effects be utilized to induce a significant glass-to-glass transition in metallic glasses, and what are the structural and thermodynamic mechanisms behind this phenomenon?. System: Equiatomic NbNiZrTiCo high-entropy metallic glass (HEMG), with comparative systems NbNiZrTiCu and NbNiZrTiCoCu. Processing: Arc melting of pure elements (Nb, Ni, Zr, Ti, Co, Cu; purity ≥ 99.9 wt.%) under high-purity argon, followed by remelting five times; ribbon production via melt-spinning at a wheel surface velocity of 32 m s−1; heat treatment by heating to 855 K (TA) at 20 K min−1 and cooling at 20 K min−1. Test conditions: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) at heating rates of 10–50 K min−1 and Flash DSC at >1000 K s−1; in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction from 305 K to 803 K at 30 K min−1; nanoindentation; dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA); atom probe tomography (APT) at 65 K; high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) at 200 kV. Findings: The as-prepared NbNiZrTiCo HEMG exhibits an enormous exothermic peak at 781 K with a heat release of 1.65 kJ mol−1, which is approximately 130% of the subsequent crystallization exotherm (1.27 kJ mol−1).; The glass-to-glass transition is irreversible; the heat-treated sample shows a distinct glass transition temperature (Tg) at ~764 K and lacks the first exothermic peak observed in the as-prepared state.; Nanoindentation measurements reveal a drastic increase in hardness from 6.78 GPa to 9.46 GPa (approximately 40% increase) after the transition.; In-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction shows a significant non-linear shift of the first peak in the total structure function S(Q) and a narrowing of the full width at half maximum (FWHM) during the transition.; Pair-distribution function (G(r)) analysis indicates a contraction of short-range atomic distances (r11 and r12 shift to low-r) and prominent splitting of the second peak, signifying enhanced short- and medium-range ordering.; Atom probe tomography confirms a uniform element distribution at the sub-nanometer scale in both as-prepared and heat-treated samples, excluding spinodal decomposition.; The calculated lower limit of entropy change (ΔSH−L) for the transition is −1.96 J mol−1 K−1, with a corresponding enthalpy change (ΔHH−L) of −1.65 kJ mol−1.; Substituting Co with Cu to form NbNiZrTiCu (maintaining high excess configurational entropy) and adding Cu to form NbNiZrTiCoCu both result in similar glass-to-glass transitions.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the high configurational entropy (SC) and high excess configurational entropy (SE) dynamically stabilize a high-energy glass state during rapid vitrification by hindering atomic reconstruction and slowing diffusion. Upon heating, this high-energy state undergoes a thermodynamically driven transition to a low-energy, more ordered glass state, releasing a large amount of heat. The transition is driven by the specific combination of high SC and high SE (related to atomic size misfit), which enables the formation of a high-energy glass that is distinct from conventional metallic glasses.. Limitations: The text notes that the observed phase transition is an irreversible process, meaning the calculated entropy change represents a lower limit. Additionally, the detailed structural changes cannot be fully resolved by atom probe tomography due to its limited spatial resolution, and some weak diffraction peaks in crystallized samples could not be identified.. Future work: The authors suggest that the HEMGs may serve as model materials for exploring glass-to-glass transitions and the fundamental nature of glasses in materials science and condensed-matter physics. They also propose potential applications as energetic materials due to the large anomalous exotherm, which could contribute to combustion heats and lower ignition temperatures.. Quote: "An unusual glass-to-glass phase transition is discovered during heating with an enormous heat release even larger than that of the following crystallization at higher temperatures."

card: Paper card. Question: How does high configurational entropy affect the correlation between calorimetric and dynamical glass transitions, and what is the underlying mechanism for the observed decoupling in high-entropy metallic glasses?. System: La55Ni20Al25, Ce55Ni20Al25, La27.5Ce27.5Ni20Al25 (LaCe-HEMG); Pd42.5Cu30Ni7.5P20, Pt57.5Cu14.7Ni5.3P22.5, Pd20Pt20Cu20Ni20P20 (PdPt-HEMG); Zr50Cu20Ni20Al10, Ti50Cu20Ni20Al10, Ti25Zr25Cu20Ni20Al10 (TiZr-HEMG). Processing: Arc-melting of raw metals (purity >99.9 mass %) in Ar atmosphere with Ti getter; melt-spinning onto a single Cu wheel at 3000 r.p.m. using Ar gas overpressure to produce glassy ribbons (thickness ~50 μm); ion milling (3 kV, then 0.5 kV with liquid nitrogen cooling) for TEM specimens. Test conditions: DSC heating rates of 0.33 K s−1 and 25–600 K s−1; DMA at 1 Hz with heating rate 0.05 K s−1 and frequencies 0.5–16 Hz; TMA heating rate 0.33 K s−1 with 0.1 N load; XRD after heating to Tx; TEM at 200 kV. Findings: LaCe-HEMG exhibits the highest α-relaxation temperature (Tα) despite having an intermediate calorimetric Tg, demonstrating decoupling between thermal and dynamic transitions.; The mixing entropy (ΔSmix) values are 1.38 R, 1.67 R, and 1.57 R for LaCe-HEMG, PdPt-HEMG, and TiZr-HEMG, respectively, all exceeding the 1.36 R threshold for high entropy.; LaCe-HEMG shows the lowest fragility (m = 35) compared to La55Ni20Al25 (m = 42) and Ce55Ni20Al25 (m = 39), indicating strong glass behavior.; The activation energy for α-relaxation (Eα) in LaCe-HEMG is 267.6 kJ mol−1, higher than Ce55Ni20Al25 (229.8 kJ mol−1) and La55Ni20Al25 (249.6 kJ mol−1).; STEM analysis reveals LaCe-HEMG has the smallest nanoscale domain size (1.851 ± 0.206 nm) compared to La55Ni20Al25 (2.491 ± 0.297 nm) and Ce55Ni20Al25 (2.380 ± 0.248 nm).; LaCe-HEMG exhibits high resistance to crystallization with few precipitates of ~8 ± 1.7 nm nanocrystals, whereas traditional MGs show widespread crystalline grains around 100 nm.; The activation energy for β-relaxation (Eβ) in LaCe-HEMG is 88.8 kJ mol−1, intermediate between Ce55Ni20Al25 (85.8 kJ mol−1) and La55Ni20Al25 (93.9 kJ mol−1).. Mechanism: The authors propose that high mixing entropy suppresses dynamic and spatial heterogeneities, leading to smaller, more homogeneous nanoscale domains (~2 nm) analogous to shear transformation zones (STZs). This homogeneity, combined with sluggish diffusion, inhibits the long-range cooperative atomic rearrangement required for α-relaxation and crystallization, thereby elevating the activation energy and Tα without significantly altering the calorimetric Tg, which is governed by local thermal diffusion.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The authors suggest that the HEA 'core effect' (sluggish diffusion on spatial heterogeneity) will provide freedom to solve fundamental issues such as the glass transition, relaxations, and aging behaviors of metallic glasses.. Quote: "HEMGs with moderate calorimetric Tg represent the highest Tα and the maximum activation energy of α-relaxation."

card: Paper card. Question: Is the 'glacial phase' in triphenyl phosphite (TPP) a distinct liquid state (liquid 2) or a mixture of glass 1 and nano-crystals, and can the liquid–liquid transition (LLT) be proven to be reversible and first-order without interference from crystallization?. System: Triphenyl phosphite (TPP), 99.7% purity. Processing: Flash differential scanning calorimetry (Flash DSC) with heating/cooling rates of 10^3 K s^-1 (1,000 K s^-1); conventional DSC with rates of 5–10 K min^-1; annealing at 216 K for up to 600 min to form glacial phase (glass 2); special temperature protocol involving quenching to 173 K, heating to Trc, holding for 0.1 s, and re-cooling.. Test conditions: Heating rates of 10^3 K s^-1 (Flash DSC) and 1/12 K s^-1 (conventional DSC); annealing temperatures of 208–216 K; annealing times (tw) ranging from 0 to 4,500 min; temperature range 173 K to >300 K; N2 atmosphere.. Findings: Ultra-high speed heating (10^3 K s^-1) successfully avoids crystallization, which occurs immediately at slower rates (e.g., 1/12 K s^-1) around 240 K.; The glacial phase prepared by annealing at 216 K for 600 min shows no glass 1 signal, confirming it is glass 2, not a mixture with glass 1.; The endothermic peak at ~250 K is attributed to the reverse LLT (liquid 2 to liquid 1) with a transition heat of ~30 J g^-1, comparable to the forward LLT heat of ~25–27 J g^-1.; For annealing above the spinodal temperature (Ta=216 K), two distinct glass transitions are observed, indicating nucleation-growth (NG) type LLT with coexisting liquid phases.; For annealing below the spinodal temperature (Ta=214 K), a single glass transition shifts continuously, indicating spinodal decomposition (SD) type LLT.; The reverse LLT occurs via an SD-type transformation with no incubation time (<0.1 s), starting immediately after the glass 2-to-liquid 2 transition gains mobility.; The stability limit of liquid 2 against liquid 1 (spinodal temperature) is estimated at ~235 K.. Mechanism: The authors propose a two-order-parameter model where LLT is a gas–liquid-like transition of the fraction of locally favoured structures (S). The transition is first-order, characterized by the coexistence of two distinct liquid states (liquid 1 and liquid 2) with different densities and order parameters. The transition type (NG or SD) depends on whether the system is in a metastable or unstable state relative to the spinodal temperatures.. Limitations: The glass 2-to-liquid 2 transition is difficult to separate from the reverse LLT because the system gains mobility and the reverse LLT initiates almost simultaneously. The spinodal temperature and stability limit are estimated indirectly and may vary with pressure.. Future work: The authors suggest their experimental method may be useful for isolating LLT from nano-crystallization in other systems like water. They propose that the critical pressure Pc exists where the two spinodal temperatures merge, and the critical temperature Tc should be located above 235 K.. Quote: "We kinetically isolate the reverse liquid-liquid transition from glass transition and crystallization with a high heating rate of flash differential scanning calorimetry"

card: Paper card. Question: How does chemical short-range order (SRO) affect the plastic response, dislocation mobility, and defect evolution during nanoindentation in the bcc HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy compared to a random alloy and an elementary Ta crystal?. System: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr (Senkov alloy) in random and short-range-ordered (SRO) states; pure Ta crystal. Processing: Molecular dynamics simulations using LAMMPS; SRO created via Monte Carlo simulation at 100 K (4.7×10^6 steps); nanoindentation with a repulsive sphere (R=10 nm) at 20 m/s to 4 nm depth, held for 100 ps, then retracted at 20 m/s; temperature maintained at 10 mK. Test conditions: Constant time step of 1 fs; bottom and lateral sides fixed; thermostat at 10 mK; indenter stiffness k=3.3 eV/Å^3; final depth d=4 nm reached at t=200 ps. Findings: The SRO alloy is 10% harder than the random HEA (H_ind increased by 10%).; The SRO alloy exhibits the highest dislocation density, remaining constant at 1.6–1.8×10^16 m^-2 throughout all phases.; The plastic zone in the SRO alloy extends farthest, with 78% of dislocations surviving retraction compared to negligible survival in Ta.; Elemental Ta shows abundant prismatic dislocation loop emission via the lasso mechanism, which is suppressed in both alloys.; The SRO alloy features zero twinning volume, whereas Ta and the random HEA show significant twinning that partially survives retraction.; The reduction in hold hardness is least for the SRO alloy (20%) compared to the elementary crystal (27%), indicating enhanced difficulty of stress relaxation.; Dislocation segment length is shortest in SRO (4.1 nm) compared to random HEA (4.7 nm) and Ta (5.8 nm).. Mechanism: The slow dislocation migration in these alloys, caused by lattice distortion and the presence of B2-ordered precipitates in the SRO state, impedes dislocation motion, prevents the formation of extended semiloops required for the lasso mechanism, and thwarts the coordinated crystal rotations necessary for twinning.. Limitations: The study uses ideal defect-free crystals with negligible initial dislocation density; the simulation temperature of 10 mK minimizes thermal vibrations but may not reflect behavior at higher temperatures where dislocation avalanches occur; the phase transformation in the SRO sample disappears after unloading, making quantification difficult.. Future work: The authors suggest that the absence of twinning in the SRO alloy might change for an alloy with larger B2 precipitates.. Quote: "Short-range order—besides making the alloy both stiffer and harder—further increases the size of the plastic zone and the dislocation density there."

Paper card. Question: How does short-range order (SRO) and the resulting B2 precipitates affect the mechanical properties, dislocation dynamics, and phase stability of a bcc HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy during nanoindentation compared to a random alloy and pure Ta?. System: HfNbTaTiZr (bcc high-entropy alloy) with and without short-range order; pure Ta crystal. Processing: Monte Carlo procedure to introduce short-range order; Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations with a volume > 20 million atoms; Nanoindentation simulation. Test conditions: Nanoindentation loading and unloading cycles; Pressure range under indenter; Comparison of random vs. SRO alloy vs. pure Ta. Findings: Short-range order causes a slight stiffening of elastic constants and an increase in indentation hardness on the 10% level.; Dislocation emission from the plastic zone is strongly impeded or absent in the alloys compared to pure Ta.; Dislocation recovery after indenter withdrawal is constrained: the plastic zone radius shrinks by 50% in pure Ta, 30% in the random alloy, and stays approximately constant in the SRO alloy.; Dislocation densities in the plastic zone are highest for the alloys, particularly the SRO alloy.; Twinning is strongest in the random alloy but shrinks to one third of its volume after unloading.; No twinning is found in the SRO alloy; instead, a limited transition to the hcp phase occurs next to the indenter.; HfTi-rich precipitates in the B2 structure impede dislocation motion and contribute to hardening.. Mechanism: The generation of HfTi-rich precipitates in the B2 structure impedes dislocation motion and helps hardening. The breaking of crystal symmetry and presence of B2 precipitates in the SRO alloy prevent the coordinated motion necessary for twin formation, favoring a limited transition to the hcp phase. Dislocation mobility is decreased in the alloys, leading to constrained recovery and higher dislocation densities.. Limitations: The text notes that distinguishing a distorted omega phase from a distorted bcc phase is difficult, and that Common Neighbor Analysis (CNA) can misidentify phases under inhomogeneous strain.. Future work: Detailed understanding of plasticity might allow design of future alloys with improved performance.. Quote: "Short-range order was introduced into the sample by a Monte Carlo procedure."

W2758161787.title: Atomistic Studies of Nanoindentation—A Review of Recent Advances

card: Paper card. Question: Which powder metallurgy processing route (CIP+sintering, HIP, swaging, or SPS) combined with subsequent deformation (HPT) yields a fully dense, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr high entropy alloy with refined microstructure and acceptable mechanical properties?. System: HfNbTaTiZr equiatomic high entropy alloy. Processing: Three initial powder types were used: (1) Elemental powders mixed for 10 h at 45 rpm, cold isostatically pressed (CIP) at 400 MPa, then sintered at 1400 °C for 16 h; (2) Mechanically alloyed (MA) powders milled for 42 h; (3) Gas atomized (AT) powders. Sintering was performed at 1400 °C for 16 h in vacuum. Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) was at 1400 °C for 2 h under 190 MPa. Swaging was at 950 °C with an envelope of beta-titanium alloy. Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) was at 1300 °C for 2 min under 80 MPa. High Pressure Torsion (HPT) was at room temperature with 2.5 GPa pressure and 15 revolutions.. Test conditions: Vickers hardness measured with 98.1 N load (ISO 6507); microstructure analyzed via LM, SEM (BSE mode), and XRD (Cu Kα); oxygen content measured by gas fusion; porosity determined by image analysis; positron lifetime spectroscopy used for defect characterization.. Findings: Swaging of sintered specimens resulted in cracking and failure, preventing full densification.; SPS of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders produced a fully dense but brittle specimen with high oxygen content (~1.07 wt %).; SPS of gas atomized (AT) powder with low oxygen content (~0.12 wt %) resulted in a fully dense, single-phase bcc specimen.; High pressure torsion (HPT) of the AT-SPS specimen refined the grain size from ~50 μm to below 500 nm (0.5 μm).; The AT-SPS-HPT specimen achieved a hardness of 410 HV10 (Abstract) and 584 HV10 (Section 4.3), attributed to grain refinement and dislocation density exceeding 5 × 10^14 m^-2.; Samples processed via CIP followed by HIP exhibited significantly lower hardness (~150 HV10) due to incomplete dissolution of elements and lack of a single-phase random solid solution.; Oxygen content above 0.8 wt % caused a sharp increase in hardness due to the formation of HfO2 particles.. Mechanism: The authors argue that oxygen contamination is the primary cause of embrittlement and prevents the formation of a single-phase random solid solution. The high oxygen content in MA powders leads to the formation of stable HfO2 oxides which cause brittleness. The single-phase bcc structure in the AT-SPS sample is attributed to the high cooling rate (~300 °C/min) during SPS, which suppresses the formation of secondary phases (bcc2 and hcp). Grain refinement and increased hardness in HPT-processed samples are caused by the formation of a high density of dislocations (>5 × 10^14 m^-2) and the presence of oxide particles in oxygen-rich samples.. Limitations: Swaging caused specimen cracking due to brittleness likely induced by high oxygen content (~0.75 wt %) or inappropriate deformation temperature/strain rate. The MA-SPS-HPT specimen broke into pieces during HPT, making its results disputable. Samples prepared by CIP and HIP retained considerable porosity and chemical inhomogeneities. The low hardness of HEAP-HIP samples could not be fully explained, though porosity and phase composition were suspected factors.. Future work: The authors state that the possibility of hot deformation of the alloy with increased oxygen content cannot be excluded under suitable conditions (i.e., low strain rate, or higher processing temperature), but this possibility needs more detailed study.. Quote: "The most promising result was obtained by SPS treatment of gas atomized powder with low oxygen content."

W3136968331.title: Anomalous dislocation core structure in shock compressed bcc high-entropy alloys

card: Paper card. Question: Can the nature and extent of local chemical ordering in high-entropy alloys be systematically controlled using binary enthalpies of mixing to enhance mechanical properties while overcoming the strength-ductility trade-off?. System: FCC CoFeNi base alloy with controlled additions of Al and Ti (CoFeNi, Al0.25CoFeNi, Al0.3CoFeNi, Al0.3Ti0.2CoFeNi) and BCC NbTaTi base alloy with Al addition (NbTaTi, Al0.5NbTaTi). Processing: Vacuum arc melting followed by homogenization and solution treatment at 1,200 °C (1 h for FCC ingots, 48 h for BCC ingots), cold rolling (50% reduction for FCC), annealing at 1,200 °C for 5 min, and water quenching; subsequent isothermal annealing at 500 °C for 0 to 5 h for ordering evolution studies. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing at a strain rate of 0.001/s for FCC alloys; room temperature compression testing at a strain rate of 0.001/s for BCC alloys. Findings: Yield strength of the near-random CoFeNi alloy was 181 MPa, increasing to 802 MPa in the Al0.3Ti0.2CoFeNi alloy with well-developed long-range order.; Tensile ductility increased from ~21% for the random CoFeNi alloy to ~76% for the Al0.3CoFeNi alloy containing early-stage long-range ordered domains.; The Al0.25CoFeNi alloy exhibited short-range ordered Ni–Al-rich clusters with an average diameter of 3 ± 1.5 nm and a yield strength of 287 MPa.; The Al0.3CoFeNi alloy showed early-stage long-range order domains of 3 ± 1.5 nm size with a yield strength of 454 MPa.; The Al0.3Ti0.2CoFeNi alloy displayed well-developed long-range ordered domains of ~8 ± 2 nm size.; In the BCC system, the Al0.5NbTaTi alloy showed a yield stress of ~1,039 MPa compared to ~587 MPa for the base NbTaTi alloy, while maintaining ~52% compressive plastic strain.; DFT calculations indicated that short-range ordering in Al0.27CoFeNi reduces total energy by 0.118 to 0.200 eV per Al atom at 1,200 °C.; Solid solution strengthening was calculated to contribute only 20 to 30 MPa, confirming that chemical ordering is the primary driver for the observed strength increase.. Mechanism: The authors argue that controlled additions of elements with large negative binary enthalpies of mixing (Al, Ti) drive the formation of short-range ordered (SRO) domains and long-range ordered (LRO) precipitates (L12 in FCC, B2 in BCC). These nanoscale ordered domains act as obstacles to dislocation motion, significantly boosting yield strength. The simultaneous increase in ductility is attributed to a deformation mechanism involving glide plane softening, localized slip in multiple {111} planes, and a dynamic Hall–Petch-like effect that refines slip length and triggers homogeneous dislocation-mediated plasticity.. Limitations: The study notes that the thermodynamic framework relies on binary enthalpies of mixing and assumes similar vibrational entropic contributions; the authors state that future studies will include vibrational entropy effects to improve accuracy. Additionally, the BCC system validation was limited to preliminary compression tests.. Future work: The authors propose that future studies will include the effects of vibrational entropy to improve the accuracy of computational results and that the detailed microscopy and fundamental deformation mechanisms of these alloys are subjects of future interest.. Quote: "Specifically, a progressively increasing local order boosts the tensile yield strengths of the parent CoFeNi alloy by a factor of four while also substantially improving ductility, which breaks the so-called strength–ductility paradox."

W4367049061.title: Molecular dynamics simulations for nanoindentation response of metastable high entropy alloy

card: Paper card. Question: How do the proportions of high-density elements Hf and Ta affect the mechanical properties (strength, elastic modulus, dislocation density) of Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr high-entropy alloys, and can a low-density composition be successfully formed via laser melting deposition (LMD) to overcome microstructural coarsening?. System: Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr high-entropy alloys, specifically HfxNbTaxTiZr (x = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) and the designed low-density Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr. Processing: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using LAMMPS with NPT system relaxation and strain rate of 4 × 10^8 s^-1; Experimental preparation via arc melting for as-cast samples and Laser Melting Deposition (LMD) using a 3 kW semiconductor laser (wavelength 900–1070 nm), laser power 600–1400 W, scanning rate 4 mm/s, powder feeding rate 8 g/min, and height increment 0.5 mm. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing at a constant displacement speed of 0.3 mm/min; XRD analysis (10~90° 2θ, 10°/min); SEM and EBSD for microstructure; Vickers hardness testing. Findings: MD simulations show that decreasing the Ta element proportion reduces the yield strength of the HEA.; Decreasing the Hf element proportion increases the yield strength of the HEA.; Simultaneously decreasing Hf and Ta ratios reduces the elastic modulus and strength, leading to microstructure coarsening in as-cast samples.; LMD processing refines the grain size of Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr from 300 μm (as-cast) to 20–80 μm (as-deposited).; The as-deposited Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr HEA exhibits a yield strength (σs) of 925 ± 9 MPa, compared to 730 ± 23 MPa for the as-cast version.; The as-deposited low-density alloy achieves strength similar to the as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr HEA (σs = 970 ± 15 MPa).; The as-deposited microstructure shows an alternating distribution of coarse columnar grains and fine equiaxed grains along the z-direction.; Dislocation density in the as-deposited alloy is higher than in as-cast samples due to thermal stress accumulation during LMD.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the strength increase in as-deposited samples to grain refinement and the Hall-Petch relation, where grain boundaries resist slip transfer. The coarsening in as-cast low-Hf/Ta alloys is explained by the reduction in these elements. The formation of columnar grains in LMD is caused by epitaxial growth from successive thermal cycles, while equiaxed grains form due to lower nucleation barriers, reducing anisotropy. Increased mechanical properties in LMD samples are also linked to the accumulation of thermal stress increasing dislocation density.. Limitations: The MD simulation model scale is too small to accurately reflect the effect of grain boundaries and grain size on alloy properties, leading to quantitative differences between simulated and actual values.. Future work: The authors suggest that while MD simulation has quantitative limitations, its qualitative analysis reduces the amount of experiments needed in component design, and combining it with additive manufacturing technology has good application prospects for engineering.. Quote: "The simultaneous decrease in the ratio of Hf and Ta elements reduces the elastic modulus and strength of HEA and leads to the coarsening of the alloy microstructure."

card: Paper card. Question: How do the addition of high-melting-point metal elements (V, Mo) and a non-metallic element (B) affect the phase composition, microstructure, mechanical properties, and fracture mechanism of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloys?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 base alloy with additions of 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 at.% V, Mo, or B. Processing: Vacuum arc melting of raw materials (>99.5% purity) with 4 iterations of repeated melting to produce ~80 g ingots, followed by stress relief annealing at 200 °C for 3 h. Test conditions: Micro-hardness tested at loads of 100, 200, 300, 500, and 1000 g (15 s dwell); tensile tests on 8 mm × 2 mm × 2 mm samples at a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Findings: The Mo0.2 alloy achieved the highest tensile strength of 1346.3 MPa and fracture elongation of 24.6%.; All alloys with V and Mo additions exhibited tensile strengths exceeding 1000 MPa.; The hardness of the B0.3 alloy reached HV498.1, which is 48% higher than the base alloy.; The FCC phase proportion decreased and then increased with V and Mo content, while it increased and then decreased with B content.; V and Mo elements were distributed in both dendritic (FCC) and interdendritic (BCC) phases.; The fracture mechanism for V and Mo alloys was mixed ductile and brittle, whereas the B-containing alloy showed cleavage fracture.; The Mo0.2 alloy showed a volume ratio of BCC to FCC phases of 28:72.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the superior properties of the Mo0.2 alloy to the coordination of deformation facilitated by fine microstructures and a high proportion of the FCC phase, which allows for plastic deformation in dendritic lamellae while cracks propagate through the BCC lamellae. For B-containing alloys, the increase in hardness is attributed to grain refinement, an increase in the proportion of the harder BCC phase, and a morphological change from lamellar eutectic to petal-like structures.. Quote: "The Mo0.2 alloy had the highest tensile strength, of 1346.3 MPa, and fracture elongation, of 24.6%."

card: Paper card. Question: How to achieve a simultaneous balance of high fracture strength and high ductility in high-entropy alloys while overcoming inferior castability and compositional segregation?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Vacuum induction melting of commercially pure elements (Al, Co, Ni: 99.9 wt.%; Cr, Fe: 99.5 ~ 99.6 wt.%) in a BN crucible; heating to 600°C for 1 hour; pouring at 1500°C into a MgO crucible (220 mm length, 62 mm upper ID, 50 mm bottom ID) under argon atmosphere (0.06 MPa); bulk ingot weight ~2.5 kg.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests at strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1; elevated temperature tests at 600°C and 700°C at strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1; cold rolling with 8% thickness reduction followed by tensile testing at 2 × 10−3 s−1.. Findings: The as-cast alloy exhibited a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure with an inter-lamellar spacing of about 2 μm.; Room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%.; The proof stress was 75 MPa, while the fracture stress reached close to 1.2 GPa (true stress condition).; At 600°C, the alloy maintained a fracture stress of 806 MPa and elongation of 33.7%.; At 700°C, the alloy maintained a fracture stress of 538 MPa and elongation of 22.9%.; Cold rolling with 8% reduction increased the true fracture stress to 1265 MPa while maintaining 9.9% elongation.; The density of the EHEA was measured to be 7.38 g/cm3.; The ratio of fracture strength to proof stress (σUTS/σ0.2) was close to 16.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the unprecedented strain hardening and balanced properties to the fine regular lamellar structure that easily stores dislocations and the alternating soft fcc phases and hard B2-structured NiAl-rich phases. When dislocations pass through soft fcc phases, the hard B2 phases, including nanoscale precipitates, pin the movement of dislocations resulting in significant work hardening.. Limitations: The text notes that the mechanism for the low elastic limit (proof stress) is still unclear at this stage.. Future work: Further exploration of new EHEAs will be based on physical metallurgy principles using atomic radius, mixing enthalpy, and valence electron concentration; thermodynamics calculations based on the CALPHAD method can provide guidance once reliable databases are established; the potential for producing ultrahigh strength components after large plastic deformation awaits further investigations.. Quote: "To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases."

card: Paper card. Question: How can cryo-rolling and annealing be utilized to overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in multiphase high entropy alloys, specifically regarding the development of a hierarchical microstructure?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Multi-pass cryo-rolling up to ~90% reduction in thickness with immersion in liquid N2 for 45 minutes before and after each pass, followed by annealing at 800 °C for 1 hour and water quenching.. Test conditions: Tensile tests at ambient temperature with an initial strain rate of 8.3 × 10−4 s−1; Nano-indentation with load increased linearly from 1 μN to 500 μN over 0.25 seconds.. Findings: The cryo-rolled and annealed material achieved a Yield Strength (YS) of 1437 ± 26 MPa and Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS) of 1562 ± 33 MPa.; The elongation to failure (ef) was approximately 14 ± 1%, which remained almost unchanged compared to the as-cast material (17 ± 1%).; The hierarchical microstructure consists of fine lamellar regions with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and coarse non-lamellar regions with coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm).; The hardness of the B2 phase (~12 GPa) is nearly three times higher than that of the L12 phase (~4 GPa) in the as-cast material.; The cryo-rolled and annealed material covers the entire hardness spectrum with softer regions (≤8 GPa), intermediate regions (~8–12 GPa), and much harder regions (≥12 GPa).; The cold-rolled and annealed material showed a homogenous microduplex morphology with grain sizes of ~0.5 µm, unlike the heterogeneous cryo-rolled structure.; The cryo-rolled and annealed EHEA possesses the highest YS and UTS while maintaining appreciable ductility compared to other HEAs like Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi and Fe40Mn27Ni26Co5Cr2.. Mechanism: The simultaneous enhancement in strength and ductility originates from a characteristic hierarchical microstructure that creates profuse domain boundaries separating domains of different hardness, leading to significant back stress strengthening and delayed necking due to strain gradients and geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs).. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The text does not explicitly state future work.. Quote: "The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%)"
